A.explanation: About $1 \text{ Pa}$ would need an area of $600 \text{ m}^2$, far larger than two feet.

B.explanation: About $100 \text{ Pa}$ would need an area of $6 \text{ m}^2$, still much larger than the contact area of shoes.

C.explanation: With total foot area of order $0.04 \text{ m}^2$, $p = F/A$ gives about $600/0.04 \approx 1.5 \times 10^4 \text{ Pa}$.

D.explanation: About $10^6 \text{ Pa}$ would need a tiny area of $0.0006 \text{ m}^2$, like a sharp pin, not flat feet.

hints: Notice the downward force on the ground is the man's weight, $600 \text{ N}$, spread over both feet flat on the ground.
Recall pressure from a solid contact is $p = F/A$, so you need a sensible estimate of the total contact area of two shoes in $\text{m}^2$.
Estimate one shoe as roughly $0.25 \text{ m}$ long by $0.08 \text{ m}$ wide and double it, then divide $600 \text{ N}$ by that total area to find the power of ten.
walkthrough: Identify the force: the man pushes on the ground with $F = 600 \text{ N}$ distributed over two feet.
State the rule: pressure is $p = F/A$, where $A$ is the total contact area in $\text{m}^2$ and $p$ is in $\text{Pa}$.
Estimate the area: one flat foot is about $0.25 \text{ m} \times 0.08 \text{ m} \approx 0.02 \text{ m}^2$, so two feet give $A \approx 0.04 \text{ m}^2$.
Calculate: $p \approx 600/0.04 = 15000 \text{ Pa}$, which is of order $10^4 \text{ Pa}$.
Compare with the options: $1 \times 10^4 \text{ Pa}$ matches this order of magnitude. This is option C.
